paper_title: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Generative simulation can automate robot environment construction, but physically valid environments are not necessarily useful for training. The challenge is to identify environments that address a policy's failures and supervision that helps it overcome them. We introduce CoDA, a framework in which a simulation data engine and an action policy co-evolve through a shared heterogeneous memory of environment construction, policy failures, and learning progress. The memory compiles validated diagnoses from a vision-language critic into generation programs that recreate difficulties and training programs that help the policy overcome them. We further propose Text2potential to convert these diagnoses into staged potentials for action-chunk value learning, providing dense supervision for policy updates while preserving the task's optimal policy under standard shaping assumptions. Measured learning progress guides further generation and program refinement. Across four manipulation task families, CoDA improves out-of-distribution success from 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning to 27.6%, exceeding the strongest closed-loop baseline by 9.5 percentage points with the same generation budget. On LIBERO-Pro, 15 rounds of generation and training raise success from 25% to 84% under position perturbations and from 1% to 76% under instruction perturbations.

sections.title: Start
sections.content: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies Tianjiao Yu1 Zhilin Ou2 Yifan Shen1 Xinzhuo Li1 Yuanzhe Liu1 Onkar Kishor Susladkar1 Fan Wang3 Ismini Lourentzou1 1University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign 2The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen 3Amazon ty41@illinois.edu lourent2@illinois.edu Generative simulation can automate robot environment construction, but physically valid environments are not necessarily useful for training. The challenge is to identify environments that address policys failures and supervision that helps it overcome them. We introduce CoDA, framework in which simulation data engine and an action policy co-evolve through shared heterogeneous memory of environment construction, policy failures, and learning progress. The memory compiles validated diagnoses from vision-language critic into generation programs that recreate difficulties and training programs that help the policy overcome them. We further propose Text2potential to convert these diagnoses into staged potentials for action-chunk value learning, providing dense supervision for policy updates while preserving the tasks optimal policy under standard shaping assumptions. Measured learning progress guides further generation and program refinement. Across four manipulation task families, CoDA improves out-ofdistribution success from 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning to 27.6%, exceeding the strongest closed-loop baseline by 9.5 percentage points with the same generation budget. On LIBERO-Pro, 15 rounds of generation and training raise success from 25% to 84% under position perturbations and from 1% to 76% under instruction perturbations. Keywords: Robot Learning, Generative Simulation, Data-Policy Co-Evolution, Shared Memory, Potential-Based Reward Shaping Website: https://plan-lab.github.io/coda Figure 1: CoDA Co-evolution of data generation and action policies. Shared memory integrates scene-construction experience and policy rollout diagnoses to guide both what environments to generate and how to train the policy. Generation programs produce environments targeting current policy difficulty modes, while training programs supply shaping potentials for policy improvement. Subsequent rollouts update the memory and guide the next round. 1. Introduction Simulation has become primary source of robot manipulation data, but building simulated environments has long been the bottleneck: each one requires task design, semantically appropriate assets, plausible layout, and training signal, often all specified by hand [38]. Generative simulation removes much of that cost. Coding agents now synthesize scenes, articulations, and task specifications directly [25, 3739, 43], and language models author the reward functions that accompany them [42, 48]. Environments are no longer scarce. central challenge remaining is deciding which environments to build next and what supervision will help the policy to learn from them. Existing engines sample variation from hand-specified ranges [29], refine scene until it is physically valid [39, 43], or allocate budget by per-task success rate [10]. These signals indicate whether an environment is valid and how well the current policy performs, but do not by themselves measure how much the policy improves through training. Without such feedback, generator risks spending its budget on environments the policy has already mastered or cannot yet learn to solve. 1 CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies CoDA closes this loop with heterogeneous memory shared by the data generator and the action policy. It records repairs needed to make scenes valid, together with policy failure diagnoses grounded in rollout evidence and localized to one generative factor and one trajectory phase. The memory tracks learning progress for recurring difficulty modes to guide subsequent generation. This evidence is compiled into separate programs for scene generation and policy training, with the latter specifying subgoals and learning tools [38, 42]. As tasks involve longer sequences of dependent subtasks, sparse success signals can slow value learning, while designing effective dense rewards can require manual effort. We therefore introduce Text2potential, which compiles failure diagnosis into potential over the simulator state and uses it to densify value targets for action chunks [7, 15]. The resulting value estimates guide policy updates through weighted regression on the policys own rollouts, favoring action chunks with higher estimated value. Across four manipulation tasks, CoDA achieves 27.6% out-of-distribution success, compared with 5.3% for the supervised fine-tuning baseline. With the same budget for generating environments, loop guided by per-task success rates achieves 18.1%, while open-loop variants yield 8.5%. Extending our loop to more rounds increases out-of-distribution success to 42.1%. Moreover, on LIBERO-Pro, training on source-task variants generated by CoDA increases success from 25% to 84% on position generalization and from 1% to 76% on task generalization. Finally, we observe that reusing memory across policy backbones transfers accumulated experience, enabling second backbone to increase out-of-distribution success from 3.8% to 21.1%. In summary, the contributions of our work are: Closed-loop co-evolution. We introduce CoDA, framework that co-evolves simulation data engine with trainable action policy. Failure diagnoses grounded in policy rollouts guide environment generation and training, while measured learning progress determines which difficulties to revisit. Shared heterogeneous memory. We introduce memory shared by the generator and policy that combines episodic evidence, reusable difficulty modes, and procedural programs. The same diagnosis compiles into generation program that recreates the difficulty and training program that helps the policy overcome it. Both programs are indexed by difficulty mode, making them reusable across tasks. Dense through supervision Text2potential. Text2potential compiles failure diagnoses into potentials over simulator states that provide dense targets for learning the value of action chunks [15]. Reward shaping requires potential evaluations only at chunk endpoints and preserves the policies that maximize the original task return. Improved out-of-distribution generalization. Across four manipulation task families, CoDA achieves 27.6% out-of-distribution success, compared with 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning and 18.1% for successrate-guided generation using the same acceptedenvironment budget. On LIBERO-Pro, fifteen rounds of CoDA training increase π0.5s success from 25% to 84% under position perturbations and from 1% to 76% under instruction perturbations. Reusing memory across policy backbones also improves OpenVLAOFTs out-of-distribution success from 3.8% to 21.1% without additional environment generation. 2. Related Work Agentic asset and scene synthesis. Recent methods improve visual asset quality [40, 50] and model part structure, articulation, or physical properties [2, 3, 13, 17, 36, 46, 47, 51]. For robot learning, RoboGen [38] generates tasks, scenes, and training supervision, while RoboTwin 2.0 [4] scales bimanual manipulation data through expert data synthesis and domain randomization. SimFoundry [29] generates variations across objects, scenes and tasks, and agentic systems automate scene construction and refinement for simulation [25, 37, 39, 43, 44]. Our work focuses on adapting environment generation to the policys learning progress, using feedback from training to guide what is generated next. Curriculum learning and policy improvement. Curriculum methods prioritize environments using regret, learning potential, or parameter changes [6, 9, 23, 27, 49]. POET [35] coevolves agents and parameterized environments, while language models synthesize rewards [19, 41, 42] and generate adaptive environment programs [10, 16]. For policy improvement, VLA policies learn from their rollouts using sparse success rewards [14, 32]. Q-Planning [7] improves action selection while keeping the base policy frozen. We adopt critic over action chunks [15] with advantage-weighted regression to update the policy [24]. Lifelong methods retain reusable prompts or skill libraries [18, 45]. CoDA links scene generation and policy learning through failure diagnoses localized to scene factors and trajectory phases. 3. Method CoDA couples scene generation and policy learning through shared memory that guides both. data engine G, implemented as tool-augmented coding agent, writes executable scene programs against simulator SDK. Each program defines an environment and machine-checkable success predicate ν. An action policy πθ collects rollouts in these environments, and vision language critic diagnoses failures by identifying the responsible factor, trajectory phase, and supporting rollout evidence. Failures intrinsic to motor execution are recorded separately from those attributed to scene factors. The memory consolidates this evidence into reusable difficulty modes. Validated modes are compiled into two complementary outputs: generation programs 2 CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies Figure 2: The CoDA framework. The data engine generates executable scenes with independently editable task, spatial, and object-attribute factors (τ, σ, α) and sparse success verifier ν. Construction traces and rollout-grounded failure diagnoses enter shared memory, which organizes them into reusable difficulty modes. Validated modes are compiled into generation programs that reproduce the diagnosed conditions and training programs that specify subgoals, potentials, and learning tools. Text2potential supplies dense feedback through chunk-level value targets that guide policy updates, and measured learning progress guides the next generation round. that recreate the diagnosed conditions and training programs that help the policy πθ overcome them. We first construct seed environments (3.1) and define the shared memory (3.2). Each round then uses the memory to guide scene generation (3.3), compiles validated diagnoses into training programs through Text2potential (3.4), and updates the policy using shaped value estimates (3.5). The resulting learning progress informs subsequent generation. Figure 2 provides an overview of the overall framework. 3.1. Seeding and Scene Representation Seeding begins with an object pool [5, 33, 51]. We use task familys assets when available and otherwise sample from predefined pool. Given the sampled objects, the engine proposes task [38] and specifies its instruction, participating objects, initial and terminal object states, and executable success predicate ν. Proposals without verifier are discarded. Instead of committing to specific data generation scheme, the engine writes factored scene programs. Task, layout, and object attributes can then be perturbed independently, letting the loop test diagnosis by changing one factor while keeping the others fixed. Failure diagnosis and scene generation need to share common representation. The critic should identify factors that the engine can directly modify. We parameterize each environment as = (τ, σ, α), generated by executing scene program = Exec(g) with G(). The task factor τ specifies the goal predicate, instruction, and initial and terminal object states. The object-spatial factor σ specifies poses, support and containment relations, clearances, and occlusion. The object self-attribute factor α specifies geometry, metric scale, mass, friction, articulation, and appearance. The SDK exposes these factors through set_task, set_layout, and set_attributes, so the engine can resample any one factor while keeping the other two fixed. This factorization provides common representation for the critics diagnoses, the engines interventions, and the applicability conditions of compiled generation programs. Verification. Each program emits sparse, machinecheckable success predicate ν over its scene objects. This predicate determines task success independently of the critics judgments and provides the common success criterion across the methods we compare. Dense training feedback is introduced separately through potential-based shaping, rather than replacing the task predicate with synthesized reward [42, 48]. Before policy deployment, each scene must pass verification checks for collision-free placement, static stability during short passive simulation, and plausible metric scale. Programs that fail these checks are excluded from policy rollouts but retained in memory to inform subsequent scene generation. 3.2. Shared Heterogeneous Memory Memory combines two sources of experience: the engines construction and repair traces, and the policys rollout outcomes and failure diagnoses. Following the episodicsemanticprocedural organization of language-agent memory [30], we retain individual records (episodic tier), abstract recurring failure patterns (semantic tier), and compile reusable programs for generation and training (procedural tier). 3 CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies Episodic tier: construction and rollout evidence. The append-only trace store records each scene program g, its verifier ν, and summaries of the generation trace, including violated constraints and verification outcomes. For deployed environments, it also records the success rate (cid:98)p(s) over rollouts and the learning progress LV(s) obtained from training [49]. The visionlanguage critic uses scene and rollout evidence to produce failure diagnosis ψ = (δ, p, c, e), where δ {TASK, SPATIAL, ATTRIBUTE, EXECUTION} identifies the attributed factor, the trajectory phase, naturallanguage description of the cause, and the supporting evidence. These diagnoses are stored alongside the corresponding traces. The additional label EXECUTION covers motor-execution failures. Semantic tier: reusable difficulty modes. Episodic records are clustered online into difficulty modes Kj using the factorphase pair (δ, p) and similarity between diagnosed causes. Each mode captures recurring failure condition that can arise across tasks and policy backbones, such as an occluder adjacent to the target on the approach side. We characterize each mode by two quantities, hardness and importance. Hardness is measured by the policys success rate (cid:98)pj, with lower rates indicating greater difficulty. Importance wj is running score updated from mode-level learning progress, measured as the change in policy success rate on that mode before and after training [49]. These two quantities reflect different properties of mode. mode can remain hard even when training on it yields little learning progress, or become easy after substantial improvement. Each mode also carries validation status determined by control batches (3.3), and only validated modes are compiled into procedural memory. Procedural tier: generation and training programs. The two consumers of memory improve differently. The data engine adapts in context by retrieving and executing programs between rounds, while the action policy πθ learns through gradient updates and acts from observations. We therefore compile the same validated mode into two complementary programs: Generation programs, stored in Ω, encode how to reproduce and vary the diagnosed scene conditions. They retain the parent scene program, validated variants along one factor, compilation-check outcomes, and the required relational structure expressed over symbolic object roles. Training programs, stored in Φ, specify how to address the policy failure through subgoal decompositions, potentials, and learning tools. They retain the diagnosed phase and evidence of which training programs improved policy performance. The generation compiler Rgrind produces the former, while Text2potential implements the training compiler Rhone (3.4). During training, these programs evaluate subgoal completion and compute potentials that shape value targets. At deployment, the trained policy predicts actions from observations and the task instruction without executing these programs. 3.3. Memory-Guided Scene Generation At each round, memory guides which difficulty modes to revisit and how to instantiate them in new environments. We allocate the generation budget across difficulty modes using an upper-confidence rule based on their hardness and observed learning progress. An ε-fraction of the budget is reserved for novel environments, while separate replay fraction revisits previously encountered modes to detect performance regressions. validated generation program is added to the pool Ω when the policys success rate on its variants falls within the designated success band and is removed when success rate is outside that band. For each selected mode, the engine retrieves generation program specifying the scene conditions to reproduce and the factor to vary. Generation programs express scene conditions in terms of symbolic object roles, allowing the engine to reuse them across task families by assigning those roles to objects in new scene (Appendix A). For each selected candidate difficulty mode linked to scene factor, the engine generates targeted batch that varies the identified factor and control batch that varies different factor. After verification checks, we evaluate the current policy on both batches. If the targeted variants yield lower policy success rate than the control variants, the proposed difficulty mode is compiled into reusable generation and training programs. The policy learns from its rollouts using the success predicate ν and the potential-based feedback supplied by Text2potential (3.4). scripted planner also attempts each valid variant, and trajectories that satisfy ν are retained as demonstrations Dt, providing additional imitation supervision when available. 3.4. Text2potential The success predicate ν determines whether generated task is complete, but provides little feedback on intermediate progress. This makes value learning difficult when success requires long sequence of actions. Text2potential converts validated failure diagnosis into subgoals and potentials over simulator states. These potentials provide dense feedback for value learning (3.5). Prior language-based reward synthesis provides dense training feedback, but its iterative refinement relies on humans to describe policy failures observed in rollouts, and can produce rewards that favor behavior other than task completion [42]. Text2potential instead uses critic to diagnose failures from the policys own rollouts and compiles these diagnoses into potential function that shapes the value critics training targets, providing dense feedback without replacing the original task reward. The compiler Rhone uses language model supplied with the failure record, the scene programs symbol table, geometric and contact helper functions, and training programs retrieved from Φ as examples. It produces the subgoal decomposition, completion predicates, potentials, and learning-tool assignments in Eq. (1). Each emitted program undergoes syntax checks and, when rollout states are supplied, runtime checks on those states. Detected errors are returned to the compiler for repair. These checks establish that the programs execute. Their usefulness is assessed through subsequent policy learning (3.5). 3.5. Policy Training The compiled potential shapes the training targets of value critic over action chunks. The value critic guides data collection and supplies the advantage estimates used to weight policy updates. This value critic is distinct from the visionlanguage critic C, which diagnoses failures. The policy must be able to sample candidate action chunks conditioned on observations and the task, (o, τ), and support weighted supervised action loss. Chunk-level value learning. The value critic Qϕ(ot, at:t+h) takes observations, the task instruction, and an action chunk as input, using visual and language encoders separate from the policys. Under these conditions, shaping preserves the policies that maximize the original task return. This property concerns exact values; the effect of shaping on the learned critic and policy is assessed through subsequent policy progress. Refinement and routing. We assess each training program by measuring the policys improvement on the corresponding difficulty mode, using ν to determine task success. We also compare how quickly the value critic converges with and without the compiled potential. If the potential provides no improvement in convergence speed over sparse task rewards alone, the visionlanguage critic revisits the failure diagnosis, and Rhone revises the subgoal decomposition. For each subgoal, we select learning procedure based on the policys measured success rate [38]. When this rate is near zero and planner demonstration is available, we use behavior cloning on Dt to teach the policy an initial solution. When the success rate falls within the target band, we use Text2potential to shape the value-learning targets. For difficulty modes with success rates above the band, we periodically re-evaluate the policy to detect performance regressions. If none of the subgoals falls within the target band, we return the difficulty mode to the data engine for further environment generation and reduce its importance score when allocating subsequent generation budgets. Scheduling. Each round generates targeted environments and their controls. After verification, we collect policy rollouts in each valid environment. The visionlanguage critic examines stratified sample of at most failed rollouts per mode. Between generation rounds, the value critic receives KQ updates and the policy receives Kπ updates using the accumulated buffer. After validation, difficulty modes are compiled into training programs for policy learning and generation programs for subsequent rounds. new generation round is triggered when fewer than eight difficulty modes remain within the success band or when learning progress plateaus for 2k policy-update steps. The loop terminates when no mode remains in the band or the generation budget is exhausted. 4. Experiments We evaluate CoDA on four Experimental Setup. manipulation task families and LIBERO-Pro [52] using π0.5 [8] as the primary policy backbone. Our main comparison includes the released π0.5 checkpoint, supervised fine-tuning on seed demonstrations, and policies trained with domain randomization, uniform environment variants [29], or success-rate-guided generation [10]. Generation baselines use the same SDK and budgets. We ablate persistent memory and the separation of generation and training stores, comparing against singlestore alternatives that include skill library [34]. We report per-suite success rates and average success across held-out suites, including generalization to unseen object instances, layouts, tasks, and categories. Additional metrics assess generation quality through verification pass rate and coverage entropy, and diagnosis quality through targeting precision, refutation rate, and agreement with two annotators on 100 sampled diagnoses. We report computational cost in LLM tokens, simulation hours, and GPU-hours per 1,000 accepted environments. Full experimental details are provided in Appendix B. Main results. Table 1 shows CoDA achieves the highest OOD success across all four task families. Average OOD success reaches 27.6%, compared with 18.1% for generation guided by task success rates and 19.2% for our critic without memory, improvements of 9.5 and 8.4 percentage points, respectively. Both substantially exceed uniform generation (8.5%) and domain randomization (7.9%), but retaining and reusing experience through our memory yields the strongest performance. In later rounds, fewer difficulty modes remain unresolved, and improvements become smaller. Removing memory produces less consistent progress, including two temporary drops in success. LIBERO-Pro. Training on generated variants of the LIBERO-Pro source tasks substantially improves robustness to position and instruction perturbations  (Table 2)  . After five rounds, CoDA achieves overall success rates of 82% and 72% under the two perturbations, respectively. Extending training to fifteen rounds raises these rates to 84% and 76%, compared with 25% and 1% for the initial π0.5 checkpoint. The fifteen-round model also exceeds ASPIRE [18] by 7 and 9 percentage points overall, achieving the highest success on the Goal and Spatial suites under both perturbations, while ASPIRE remains strongest on the Object suite. These robustness gains preserve performance on standard LIBERO, where success reaches 97.4%, compared with 97.1% before adaptation. Sensitivity to the failure diagnosis critic. Table 3 varies the visionlanguage model used to diagnose failures while keeping the engine and compiler fixed. Replacing GPT-5.5 with Claude Opus 5, InternVL3-78B, or Qwen3VL-235B slightly reduces OOD success from 27.6% to 26.1%, 25.7%, and 24.9%, respectively. Models with lower agreement with human annotators also produce more diagnoses rejected by the control tests. Nevertheless, all four models outperform generation guided by task success rates: even Qwen3-VL-235B exceeds that baseline by 6.8 percentage points. The framework therefore remains effective across the tested diagnosis models. Effect of Text2potential. Text2potential achieves 27.6% OOD success at fixed training budget, compared with 22.3% using sparse task rewards alone  (Table 4)  . It reaches 25% OOD success after 21k policy updates, compared with 31k for sparse rewards, requiring approximately 32% fewer updates. The ablations show that both failure diagnosis and potential refinement matter. Generating the potential from the task description instead of the failure diagnosis lowers success to 24.6%, while disabling refinement lowers it to 26.1%. Keeping the policy frozen and using the value critic only to select action chunks achieves 21.4%, showing the benefit of using the learned values to update the policy. Qualitative results. sections.title: Task Families
sections.content: A generation program can be reused in new task family when its object requirements and relational constraints are satisfied in the new scene. We call this transfer lifting. Each program refers to objects by symbolic role, such as target, obstacle, or support, rather than by specific object instance. Each role specifies required object category, such as container, or an affordance, such as graspable. The program also specifies the relations required between these roles, such as an obstacle occupying the approach path to the target. To apply program to new scene, Rgrind matches these requirements against the scene programs symbol table, which records object identifiers, categories, affordances, poses, and relations. This information is available directly because the data engine constructs the scene program. valid binding assigns each role to distinct scene object and satisfies all role requirements and relational constraints. If no valid binding exists, the program is not transferred to that scene. Matching is exhaustive: our programs contain at most five roles and our scenes contain few dozen objects, with matching taking milliseconds in this setting. When several bindings are valid, they are ranked first by how closely their object categories match those in the difficulty modes previously validated variants. Ties are broken using the margins by which the relational constraints are satisfied. We retain at most three bindings and execute the generation program separately for each, producing scene variant and its own matched control batch. Transferred programs undergo the same validation as programs learned within the new task family. Their generated variants must pass the scene-validity checks, and policy rollouts evaluate both the targeted variants and their controls. transferred program enters Ω for the new family only when the control comparison supports the attributed difficulty and the measured success rates of its variants fall within the success band. Thus, matching establishes whether program is applicable to the new scene; evaluation establishes whether it reproduces useful training difficulty. B. Implementation Details Environments and evaluation. We construct MuJoCo environments for four task families: pick-and-place, articulated open/close, put-inside, and stack/insert. Each family includes an in-distribution evaluation suite and four held-out suites of 100 environments each, testing generalization to unseen object instances, layouts, tasks, and categories, respectively. Held-out environments never enter M. In second setting, we initialize the loop with the 30 LIBERO source tasks and evaluate on LIBERO-Pro [52]  (Table 2)  . All results are reported as mean standard error over three random seeds. Assets, observations, and actions. The asset collection comprises 1,200 rigid objects from Objaverse across 60 categories, 300 articulated objects from ArtiCraft-10K, and 500 seed layouts from TableVerse [5, 33, 51]. The robot is 7-DoF Franka Panda with front and wrist cameras, each providing 224 224 RGB observations. Control runs at 10 Hz using seven-dimensional actions: six dimensions for the change in end-effector pose and one for the gripper command. Each action chunk contains = 8 control steps. Policy backbones. Our primary policy is π0.5, 3Bparameter model with flow-matching action head [8]. We initialize it from the released openpi base checkpoint, or from its LIBERO-fine-tuned checkpoint for the LIBERO experiments [26]. We also evaluate the 7B-parameter OpenVLA-OFT [12] in table 7. Both policies are finetuned using LoRA with rank 32 and learning rate of 105. At each rollout decision, the policy samples = 8 candidate action chunks. These are combined using softmax weights computed from Qϕ, with temperature 0.5. Scene generation, diagnosis, and potential compilation. The data engine, rollout-diagnosis model, and potential compiler all use GPT-5.5 [21]. Planner-certified demonstrations are obtained using cuRobo [31]. The diagnosis model receives rollout video, contact information, joint states, and the task success verifiers output at each timestep. It assigns each diagnosed failure to one of four factors (TASK, SPATIAL, ATTRIBUTE, or EXECUTION) and one of five trajectory phases (approach, grasp, transport, place or insert, and release). For potential compilation, Text2potential retrieves three exemplar programs from Φ and uses library of 12 helper functions. Generated programs undergo at most two rounds of repair for syntax or runtime errors. Value learning and policy optimization. The value critic Qϕ uses frozen DINOv2-B [22] and T5-base [28] encoders followed by four-layer transformer decoder. It is trained by categorical value regression with 101 bins spanning [βmmax, 1], where β = 0.5 is the shaping coefficient and mmax = 4 is the maximum number of subgoals. We use discount factor of γ = 0.99 and an exponential moving average target network with update coefficient τ = 0.005. Each round includes KQ = 20,000 critic-update steps with batch size 256 and Kπ = 5,000 policy-update steps with batch size 64. The advantage-weighted policy update uses λ = 1. Generation budgets and rollout protocol. Experiments use = 5 rounds, with per-family budgets of 320 accepted environments, 1,280 planner-certified demonstrations, and 2.5M LLM tokens. Token counts include scene generation, diagnosis, and potential compilation. Extended runs use = 15 rounds. Each round generates = 64 targeted environments and 64 control environments per task family. The policy is evaluated on each environment using = 16 rollouts from the same initial simulator state. The diagnosis model processes at most = 32 failed rollouts per difficulty mode. The success 12 CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies Table 5: Effect of memory design on policy learning. We reserve fraction ε = 0.15 of the generation budget for novel environments and 0.10 for replay, and use an upper-confidence-bound exploration coefficient of 1 when selecting difficulty modes. Round scheduling and randomization. new round is triggered when fewer than eight difficulty modes remain within the success band, or when success on modes within the band changes by less than two percentage points over the preceding 2,000 policy-update steps. The three random seeds jointly vary environment generation, policy rollouts, and model training. C. Additional Experiments Complementary generation and training programs. Table 5 evaluates the contributions of the generation and training programs retained in memory. Retaining only scene generation programs raises OOD success from 19.2% to 22.8%, while retaining only policy training programs raises it to 22.1%. Retaining both reaches 27.6%: the resulting 8.4-percentage-point improvement exceeds the sum of the individual gains, 3.6 and 2.9 points. The three baseline variants that reuse the same memory representation for both scene generation and policy training perform worse than retaining either type of specialized program alone. With both generation and training programs, the policy reaches 25% OOD success in five rounds, compared with fourteen rounds without memory. Transfer across task families. Table 6 evaluates generation programs transferred to different task family by rebinding their object roles, without relearning the programs. The baseline learns programs from scratch in the target family using the same LLM token budget as transfer. Averaged across all cross-family transfers, reused programs achieve 60.3% of the learning progress obtained with programs learned within the target family, compared with 35.8% for the from-scratch baseline. This advantage holds in every cross-family comparison, demonstrating that generation experience can be reused to support policy learning in new task families. Transfer across policy backbones. Table 7 evaluates whether memory collected with one policy backbone can support training another, with the memory held fixed and no additional environment generation. Transferred memory improves OOD success by an average of 18.9 percentage points over the SFT baseline without memory. In both transfer directions, performance remains within two percentage points of running the full framework with the target backbone. These results show that the accumulated difficulty modes and programs can support policy learning beyond the backbone used to collect them. Learning speed, action agreement, and performance as memory accumulates. On the same generated data, potential shaping accelerates policy learning relative to sparse-only training (Figure 5(a,b)). Both conditions reach similar final in-distribution success rates, but shaping reaches this level approximately 20,000 policy-update steps earlier. At the end of training, the two value critics select the same action chunk in 97% of comparisons. Figure 5(c) tracks OOD success at successive memory snapshots during training. Success increases as more difficulty modes are validated and recorded. Retaining both scene generation and policy training programs achieves the highest final success, approximately ten percentage points above retaining either program type alone. Generation quality and diagnosis validation. Table 8 shows that 88.9% of scene proposals pass the physical validity checks, compared with 71.3% under uniform sampling. Coverage entropy remains close to that of uniform sampling (3.18 versus 3.42 bits), while targeting precision increases from 24.6% to 66.7%. The engine therefore improves scene validity and targeting while maintaining broad coverage. We reject 18.2% of the critics failure diagnoses because variants that modify the identified scene factor are no harder than control variants that modify different factor. In the evaluation with two annotators and 100 sampled diagnoses, this validation step improves agreement with human annotations from 73.6% to 82.4%. Computational cost and adaptive scheduling. CoDA improves OOD success from 18.1% to 27.6% over scalar Its feedback, 52% relative improvement  (Table 9)  . computational requirements are 7.4M LLM tokens and 66 GPU-hours per 1,000 accepted environments. Adaptive scheduling improves efficiency, reducing both token usage and GPU time by approximately 11% relative to fixed round intervals while increasing OOD success from 26.1% to 27.6%. Thus, adapting when to generate new environments reduces computational cost while improving policy performance. Qualitative results. Figure 6 illustrates the scene variations produced by the data engine from four seed scenes. For each seed, we show three spatial perturbations of increasing magnitude, target-size change, and targetobject replacement. All displayed variants pass the scenevalidity checks. Additional successful policy rollouts on LIBERO-Pro tasks and generated fruit preparation scenes are shown in Figure 7. 14 CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies Table 9: Computational cost and effect of round scheduling. Four examples show changes in object layout, size, and identity for tool sorting, serving-board arrangement, craft-station organization, and noodle preparation tasks. Each panel contains seed scene, three spatial perturbations of increasing magnitude, target-size change, and target-object replacement. All displayed variants pass validity checks. D. Limitations CoDA relies on foundation models for scene generation, failure diagnosis, and potential compilation. Errors in these models understanding of objects, physical interactions, or task requirements can affect the resulting scenes and training signals. Physical validity checks and control experiments help detect such errors, but their coverage depends on the checks and interventions used. Results may also vary with changes to the underlying models, making model versions and configurations important for reproducibility. The framework requires additional simulation and model inference to generate environments, evaluate policy rollouts, and validate diagnoses. These costs constrain the number of rounds and task families that can be explored under fixed budget. Our evaluation also focuses on simulated manipulation. Broader Impact The ability to generate environments and training signals automatically has far-reaching implications for robot learning, simulation, and embodied AI. CoDA contributes to this space by turning environment generation into closed loop that responds to what policy has learned, which lowers the cost of producing diverse, verifiable training data. This can accelerate the development of capable manipulation policies, improve the fidelity and coverage of simulated benchmarks, and support scalable data generation for research groups without large teleoperation budgets. While lowering the barrier to training capable robot policies raises potential concerns about misuse and about biases inherited from the underlying foundation models, our framework is designed for research use, judges success only through machinecheckable verifiers, and audits every automated diagnosis with control experiments. We encourage responsible deployment practices that keep such audits in place. Compared to collecting real-robot demonstrations at scale, the approach is computationally efficient and requires no physical data collection, and we view its benefits in controllable, verifiable data generation as outweighing its risks when applied responsibly.
